rationale.n: Rationale is a noun meaning the reasons behind a decision, plan or belief, and it is usually followed by behind or for: the rationale behind the policy. Do not confuse it with rational, the adjective, even though they are related. It is formal and common in reports, proposals and academic writing, where you explain why something is done. It is usually singular: the rationale, a clear rationale. Stress falls on the third syllable: rash-uh-NAHL in British English, rash-uh-NAL in American English.
x: The manager explained the rationale behind moving the whole team to a new office.
I understand the rationale for the change, but I still think it is risky.

renaissance.n: The Renaissance is the period of renewed interest in art, science and learning that began in Italy in the fourteenth century and spread through Europe. Write it with a capital R when it names that period, and use it as an adjective in Renaissance art or the Italian Renaissance. With a small r it can describe any revival, such as a renaissance in local cooking. It comes from French and means rebirth.
x: Many of the greatest paintings in the museum come from the Renaissance period.
The city is enjoying a cultural renaissance, with new theatres and galleries opening.

rivalry.n: Rivalry is a continuing competition between two people, teams or organisations, and it is often friendly but intense: a fierce rivalry between two clubs. It is countable and uncountable, so you can talk about a rivalry or about rivalry in general. The prepositions are between and with: rivalry between brothers, rivalry with a neighbouring town. The person is a rival, and the verb is rival, meaning to be equal to. Stress falls on the first syllable: RY-vul-ree. It is common in sport and business.
x: The rivalry between the two football clubs goes back more than a hundred years.
There was a friendly rivalry among the students to finish the project first.

stipend.n: A stipend is a fixed regular sum paid to a student, trainee or clergy member to cover living costs, and unlike a salary it is not payment for a specific job. It is commonly used in graduate programmes and internships, where a monthly stipend helps pay for food and rent. It is countable, with the plural stipends. You receive, get or are paid a stipend, and the amount is described as modest, generous or small. Stress falls on the first syllable: STY-pend.
x: Doctoral students at the university receive a monthly stipend to cover their living costs.
The internship is unpaid, but there is a small stipend for travel and lunch.

sublet.n: Sublet is a verb for renting to someone else a property that you yourself rent, and you can do it with all or part of it: sublet a room. The forms are the same in the past and participle: sublet, sublet, subletting, with a double t. It can also be a noun, as in a summer sublet. Check that your landlord allows this first, because many contracts forbid it. The person renting from you is a subtenant. The noun is stressed SUB-let, while the verb is often sub-LET.
x: I plan to sublet my flat for three months while I work abroad.
They had to sublet the spare room to cover the rising rent.

tech-savvy.n: Tech-savvy describes someone who knows a lot about modern technology and uses it with confidence. It is informal and hyphenated, as in a tech-savvy generation or tech-savvy customers. Savvy alone means practical knowledge or good judgement, and it can combine with other words, such as business-savvy or media-savvy. Do not write it as two separate words without a hyphen when it comes before a noun. Savvy has a short a, as in cat: SAV-ee. It is common in advertising and news.
x: Tech-savvy shoppers often compare prices on three different apps before buying anything.
My grandmother is surprisingly tech-savvy and often fixes my parents' computer.

threshold.n: Threshold is the level or point at which something starts to happen or change, and it appears in many contexts: the pain threshold, the tax threshold, the threshold of a new era. It also literally means the bottom of a doorway. Typical verbs are reach, cross and exceed a threshold. It is countable, with the plural thresholds. It is spelled with only one h in the middle, but said THRESH-hohld, with stress on the first syllable.
x: Workers earning below a certain threshold do not have to pay this tax.
Some people have a much higher pain threshold than others, even without training.

dialect.n: A dialect is a form of a language spoken in one area or by one social group, with its own words, grammar and pronunciation: a regional dialect. It is not the same as an accent, which only concerns pronunciation. Many speakers use both a standard form and a local dialect. The word is countable and is usually described with local or regional. The adjective is dialectal, which is rare. Stress falls on the first syllable: DY-uh-lekt. Linguists do not consider dialects less correct than a standard language.
x: Even within a small country, people may speak a very different dialect from region to region.
He switches to the local dialect whenever he visits his grandparents in the village.

generate.n: Generate means to produce or create something, such as electricity, heat, income, interest or ideas. In the energy sense: wind turbines generate power. It is a transitive verb, so it always takes an object, and it is more formal than make. The noun is generation, which also means a group of people born around the same time. The adjective generative exists in linguistics. Stress falls on the first syllable: JEN-uh-rayt. Typical phrases include generate electricity, generate income and generate interest.
x: The new solar farm will generate enough electricity to power ten thousand homes.
The advertising campaign generated a lot of interest among younger customers.

vibrant.n: Vibrant describes places, people, cultures and bright colours that are full of energy and life, and it has a positive, lively tone. You can have a vibrant city, a vibrant community or vibrant colours. It is stronger than lively and is common in travel writing and reviews. The noun is vibrancy. Do not confuse it with vibrating, which describes shaking. Stress falls on the first syllable: VY-brunt. It is also used for sound, meaning strong and clear, as in a vibrant voice.
x: The old town has a vibrant nightlife, with live music in nearly every bar.
She painted the room in vibrant shades of orange and yellow.

aggregate.n: Aggregate as an adjective means made up of several amounts added together, and it is common in economics and statistics: aggregate demand, aggregate data. As a noun it means a total, and in building it refers to sand and stones used in concrete. The verb, meaning to combine into one total, is pronounced differently from the adjective and noun. The adjective and noun have a weak ending: AG-ruh-git, while the verb ends with a full vowel, AG-ruh-gayt. The phrase in the aggregate means taken as a whole.
x: Aggregate demand fell sharply during the recession as people spent less money.
The team will aggregate the data from all the hospitals before drawing conclusions.

i suppose.n: I suppose is used when giving an opinion or agreement that you are not very sure about, and it often sounds hesitant or slightly reluctant. It can start a sentence, or be a reply: I suppose so. The negative is I don't suppose, and you can also say I suppose that followed by a clause. It is informal and conversational, so avoid it in formal writing, where you can use presumably. Do not confuse it with suppose in the sense of imagine, as in suppose we meet at six.
x: I suppose we could leave early if the traffic gets worse tonight.
It was a good film, I suppose, but I expected much more from it.

in addition.n: In addition is a linking phrase that introduces an extra point, and it works at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma. Notice the rule on to: in addition to is followed by a noun or an ing form, as in in addition to working, and it does not take a full clause. The plain version, in addition, stands alone. It is formal and a good alternative to also in essays. Additionally is a one-word alternative with the same meaning.
x: The hotel has a gym. In addition, guests can use the swimming pool for free.
In addition to English, she speaks fluent Italian and a little Japanese.

lean over.n: Lean over is a phrasal verb meaning to bend your body forward across something or towards someone: lean over the table, lean over the edge. It is often followed by a preposition or a noun, and you can add to plus a verb to show purpose. The past form is leaned over, or leant over in British English. Compare bend over, which lowers the upper body without necessarily resting on something, and lean on, which gives support. Pronounce lean with a long vowel like "clean".
x: He had to lean over the table to reach the plate on the other side.
Please do not lean over the railing because the water below is very deep.

yours faithfully.n: Yours faithfully is a formal British way to end a letter that begins with Dear Sir or Madam, when you do not know the person's name. If you know the name, use Yours sincerely instead. After the closing, leave space for your signature and then print your full name. In American English, the common choices are Sincerely or Yours truly, so this form is mostly British. Notice that only the first word is capitalised and a comma follows the phrase.
x: Letters to an unknown reader usually end with the phrase Yours faithfully.
If the letter starts with Dear Sir or Madam, end it with Yours faithfully.

discount.n: Discount is a noun, and it is also a verb. As a noun it means an amount taken off the usual price: offer a discount, get a discount, at a discount. It is followed by on: a ten percent discount on shoes. Stress falls on the first syllable for the noun: DIS-kownt. As a verb it can mean to reduce a price, discounted goods, or to treat something as unimportant, often stressed on the second syllable: dis-KOWNT. Compare reduction, which is more formal, and sale, which describes a period of lower prices.
x: Students can get a thirty percent discount on train tickets with a valid card.
The shop offers a small discount if you pay in cash rather than by card.

acquire.n: Acquire means to get or gain something, especially knowledge, skills, possessions or a business. It is more formal than get and suggests effort or a process, as in acquire a new language. Companies acquire other companies, and the noun is acquisition. Do not confuse it with require, which means to need. The adjective acquired describes something learned, not inborn: an acquired taste. Stress falls on the second syllable: uh-KWYR.
x: Children acquire their first language naturally, simply by listening to the people around them.
The software company plans to acquire a smaller rival in the next two months.

adequate.n: Adequate means enough or good enough for a particular need, and it can sound neutral, formal or lukewarm. In reviews, adequate can mean just acceptable, not good, so a hotel described as adequate is probably disappointing. In reports it simply means sufficient, as in adequate funding. The opposite is inadequate, which is stronger and negative. It is often followed by for or to: adequate for our needs. Stress falls on the first syllable: AD-i-kwit. The adverb is adequately, and the noun is adequacy.
x: Many villages still do not have an adequate supply of clean drinking water.
The room was adequate, though a little small, and the staff were helpful.

assume.n: Assume means to accept something as true without proof: widely assumed, reasonable to assume. It is followed by a that clause or a to-infinitive in the passive: he is assumed to be innocent. It is stronger than guess, and similar to suppose, but more formal. Another meaning is to take responsibility or a role: assume control. Do not mix it up with presume, which can suggest more evidence. Stress falls on the second syllable: uh-SYOOM, and the noun is assumption.
x: Many people assume that older workers cannot learn new technology very quickly.
Let us assume for a moment that the price of fuel doubles next year.

compound.n: Compound has several meanings, and the stress changes with the grammar. As a noun, a compound is a substance made of two or more elements, such as water, or a word made from two others, such as toothbrush. It can also mean a group of buildings with a fence around them, a prison compound. As a verb, meaning to make worse, the stress shifts: com-POUND the problem. The noun and adjective are stressed on the first syllable: KOM-pownd. Chemical compound is a common phrase.
x: Water is a compound made of two atoms of hydrogen and one of oxygen.
Rising prices only compound the problems faced by families on low incomes.

conflict.n: Conflict is a serious disagreement or fighting, between people, groups or countries, and it can also describe an opposition between ideas or interests: a conflict of interest. As a noun, stress is on the first syllable: KON-flikt. As a verb, meaning to be in opposition, the stress moves to the second: kun-FLIKT, as in two reports that conflict. Typical verbs are resolve, avoid and cause conflict. It can be countable or uncountable. It is stronger than argument but less physical than war.
x: The two countries are trying to resolve the conflict through peaceful negotiation.
His work schedule is in conflict with the evening classes he wants to join.

constitute.n: Constitute means to form or be considered as something, and it is a formal verb used in analysis and law. Its meaning is similar to make up or amount to: these actions constitute a threat, women constitute a majority of students. It does not take the progressive form in this sense. The related noun is constitution, which refers to the basic laws of a state or the make-up of something. Stress falls on the first syllable: KON-sti-tyoot.
x: The authorities decided that the messages did not constitute a crime in this case.
Foreign students constitute nearly a third of the total number at the college.

facilitate.n: Facilitate means to make an action or process easier, and it is a formal verb whose object is usually a process, not a person: facilitate learning, not "facilitate the students". The subject is often a tool, a policy or a person leading a meeting, the facilitator. The noun is facilitation. Do not use it to mean just help someone personally. Typical phrases include facilitate trade and facilitate discussion. Stress falls on the second syllable: fuh-SIL-i-tayt.
x: The new app is designed to facilitate communication between teachers and parents.
A trained leader will facilitate the discussion and keep everyone on topic.

forthcoming.n: Forthcoming has three meanings. The first is about the future: a forthcoming election or forthcoming report is one that will happen or appear soon. The second means available when needed, and it is usually in negative sentences: no help was forthcoming. A third meaning, being open in giving information, describes a person who is willing to talk. It is formal. Do not hyphenate it. Stress falls on the second syllable: forth-KUM-ing, with a clear th sound at the start.
x: The author's forthcoming book will be published in the spring of next year.
We waited for hours, but no explanation was forthcoming from the airline.

incorporate.n: Incorporate means to include something as part of a whole, and it is typically used for ideas, features or changes: incorporate new ideas into a plan. The preposition is into or in, or sometimes within: incorporate feedback into the design. It also has a legal sense, meaning to form a company, with incorporated shortened to Inc in company names. The verb ends with a full "ayt" sound: in-KOR-puh-rayt, with stress on the second syllable. The noun is incorporation, and the adjective is incorporated.
x: The designers tried to incorporate the customers' suggestions into the final version.
We hope to incorporate more outdoor activities into the school timetable next term.

insert.n: Insert as a verb means to put something inside or into something else, such as a key in a lock or a clause in a contract. It is followed by into or in: insert a coin into the slot. As a noun, an insert is something added, like a leaflet in a magazine, and the stress changes: the noun is IN-sert, while the verb is in-SERT. In computing, the insert key and insert command add content. The noun insertion describes the act of inserting.
x: You must insert a coin into the machine before choosing your drink.
Please insert a new paragraph here to explain how the survey was done.

invoke.n: Invoke means to mention a law, idea or person to support an argument, or to call on a power or spirit. It is formal: invoke a law, invoke the principle of fairness. In computing, to invoke a function means to call it so that it runs. Do not confuse it with evoke, which means to bring a feeling or memory to mind. The noun is invocation. Stress falls on the second syllable: in-VOHK, and the o sound is long.
x: The lawyer decided to invoke an old law that protects the rights of tenants.
Politicians often invoke the memory of past leaders to win the public's trust.

credentials.n: Credentials are the qualifications, training and experience that show a person is suitable for a job or role, and the word is almost always plural: impressive credentials, check someone's credentials. In computing, credentials also means a username and password used to log in, as in enter your login credentials. The singular a credential is rare, though American English uses it for a professional certificate. The related word credibility means being believable, and credit has a different, financial sense. Stress falls on the second syllable: kri-DEN-shulz. It is neutral to formal.
x: The new director has impressive credentials, including twenty years in international banking.
Reporters should always check the credentials of experts before quoting their opinions.

erosion.n: Erosion is the gradual wearing away of rock or soil by water, wind or ice, and it is an uncountable noun in geography: soil erosion, coastal erosion. It also works figuratively for a slow loss of something valuable, such as the erosion of trust or rights. The verb is erode, and the adjective is erosive. Use of with the thing that is lost: erosion of confidence. Stress falls on the second syllable: i-ROH-zhun, and the s sounds like the s in vision.
x: Heavy rain and strong winds have caused serious erosion along the northern coast.
Constant criticism led to a slow erosion of her confidence at work.

inevitable.n: Inevitable describes something that you cannot avoid or prevent, and it can be neutral or negative: an inevitable consequence. It is often used with be, as in it was inevitable that something would happen, and the noun phrase the inevitable means something certain to occur. The adverb is inevitably, and the noun is inevitability. Unavoidable is a close synonym and slightly more everyday. Stress falls on the second syllable: in-EV-i-tuh-bul, and learners often drop one syllable.
x: With so many cars on the road, traffic jams are almost inevitable at rush hour.
It was inevitable that the old factory would close once cheaper imports arrived.

justify.n: When you justify a decision, a cost or an action, you show that it is reasonable, so the verb always needs a direct object. Common patterns are "justify doing something" and "justify the expense", and the adjective is justified ("a justified complaint"). The noun is justification, usually followed by for: "there is no justification for this delay". Be careful not to confuse it with excuse. If you justify something, you give reasons that show it is fair or necessary, while excuse often suggests you are avoiding blame. It is common in essays, reports and arguments where you defend a choice with evidence.
x: The council could not justify raising parking fees without improving public transport.
Nothing can justify the use of violence against peaceful protesters.

practitioner.n: Practitioner is a fairly formal noun for someone who actively works in a profession, especially medicine or law, as opposed to someone who only studies it. It is often used with a field: a legal practitioner, a medical practitioner, or a general practitioner, which is shortened to GP in British English. It can also describe a person who regularly does an activity or method, such as a practitioner of yoga. Notice the stress on the second syllable: prac-TI-tion-er. In everyday speech people often just say doctor, lawyer or professional, so keep practitioner for reports and official writing.
x: Experienced practitioners often disagree about the best way to treat chronic back pain.
The clinic employs several practitioners trained in traditional and modern medicine.

temporary.n: Temporary describes something that lasts only for a limited time, and its opposite is permanent. It is common with work and housing: a temporary job, a temporary address, a temporary contract. It often appears in the pattern "on a temporary basis", which sounds more formal. A temporary measure is a quick solution used until a proper one is found. Use provisional when something is officially accepted for now but may change, for example a provisional licence.
x: The road will stay closed as a temporary measure while engineers check the bridge.
She took a temporary position at the library to cover a colleague's maternity leave.

assess.n: Assess takes a direct object and means to judge the quality, size or importance of something after careful thought. Typical objects are risk, damage, impact, needs and performance: "assess the risk". Do not add a preposition after it, because "assess about" is not used. The noun is assessment, and a person who does this work may be called an assessor. Assess is close to evaluate, but it is often used for official checks, such as a teacher assessing coursework or an insurer assessing the damage to a car. Note the double s in both the verb and the noun.
x: Inspectors visited the farm to assess how much damage the flood had caused.
Teachers assess students through coursework as well as a final written exam.

dynamic.n: Dynamic is usually a positive adjective for people, places or systems that are active, energetic and ready to change. You can describe a dynamic leader, a dynamic economy or a dynamic city. In science, computing and business it has a more technical meaning, referring to something that changes over time, such as dynamic pricing or a dynamic website. It is also a noun, often plural: group dynamics means how people in a group affect each other. The opposite in most contexts is static.
x: The company is looking for a dynamic manager who enjoys working under pressure.
Group dynamics can change quickly when a new member joins the team.

valid.n: Valid has two main senses. In argument it means reasonable and logical, as in a valid point or a valid reason. In official contexts it means acceptable by law or by the rules: a valid passport, a valid ticket, a valid password. Both senses share the opposite invalid, as in an invalid argument or an invalid ticket. The noun is validity, and the verb is validate. In essays, "that is a valid point" is a polite way of accepting part of someone's argument. A ticket or card is valid for a period, so use the preposition for: valid for one year.
x: Your driving licence must be valid for the whole period of the rental.
He made a valid point about the lack of evidence, so we reviewed the data again.

visible.n: Visible describes something that can be seen, and it combines with adverbs such as clearly, barely, highly and partially. Beyond physical sight, it can mean easy to notice: a visible improvement, a visible effect. The opposite is invisible. The noun is visibility, which also means how far you can see in fog or rain: "visibility was poor". In workplaces, a visible leader is one who is seen and known by staff. Useful phrases with prepositions are "visible to the naked eye" and "visible from space".
x: The old city walls are still visible from the top of the hill.
Thick fog made the road barely visible, so several drivers were told to slow down.

address a concern.n: Address a concern means to deal with a worry or complaint that someone has raised, and it sounds professional, so it is common in business letters and meetings. Here address is a verb meaning to give attention to, not to write an address. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition: address concerns, address a problem, address an issue. The topic usually follows with about: a concern about safety. A plural is usual in general statements: "We want to address any concerns you may have." Note that addressing a concern does not always mean solving it fully; it means you take it seriously and respond.
x: If you have a question or would like us to address a concern, please email our support team.
The manager phoned me the next day to address a concern I had raised about overtime.

definite.n: Definite means clear, fixed and certain, and it is used for things that are decided rather than uncertain: a definite answer, a definite plan, a definite improvement. Remember the spelling, which ends in -ite, not -ate. It is often used in negative sentences: "there is no definite date yet". The adverb definitely is common in speech for strong agreement, as in "Definitely!". Do not confuse definite with definitive, which means final and authoritative, as in a definitive biography. The definite article is the grammar name for the word the.
x: We have not set a definite date for the opening, so please check the website regularly.
There has been a definite improvement in her pronunciation since she moved to Dublin.

dynasty.n: Dynasty refers to a line of rulers from the same family, and it is used for countries and also for families who keep power in business or politics. In history writing, it usually appears before or after a name: the Ming dynasty, or the dynasty of the Ptolemies. Typical verbs are found, rule and fall: "the dynasty ruled for three centuries". The stress falls on the first syllable: British speakers usually say DIN-uh-stee and Americans DY-nuh-stee. The adjective is dynastic. Do not use it for a single ruler or a short period of government; it needs several generations.
x: The Han dynasty ruled China for roughly four centuries and expanded the empire westward.
In business, a family dynasty often loses its influence when the founder's grandchildren take over.

in comparison.n: In comparison is used to point out a difference between two things, and it often begins a sentence followed by a comma. The common patterns are "in comparison with" and "in comparison to", both accepted, plus the shorter "by comparison". It is typical in describing charts and data: "In comparison, sales in Spain rose only slightly." Remember that comparison needs two items, and the second one usually follows with: "Prices are low in comparison with those in London." It is a little more formal than compared to and very common in reports and essays.
x: Rents in the capital are very high in comparison with those in smaller towns.
My old phone was heavy and slow; the new one feels light in comparison.

multilingual.n: Multilingual describes a person, community or text that uses several languages, usually more than two. It is written as one word with no hyphen. It can describe people (a multilingual teacher), places (a multilingual city), and materials (multilingual signs or websites). Compare it with bilingual for two languages and trilingual for three. The related noun is multilingualism, which is the ability to use several languages or the situation where they are all used. Stress is on the second syllable, mul-ti-LING-gwal. Employers often list it as an advantage in job advertisements.
x: The airport has multilingual signs so visitors can find the exits easily.
Growing up in a multilingual household helped her switch between languages naturally.

non-refundable.n: Non-refundable describes money that will not be returned once you have paid it, and you see it on tickets, deposits and fees. It is usually written with a hyphen, though American English also uses nonrefundable. It usually comes before a noun: a non-refundable deposit. The opposite is refundable, and the noun is refund. Remember to read this condition before booking, because you may lose the money if you cancel. A related phrase is "no refunds". When the verb is used, you refund someone or refund an amount: "We will refund your payment within ten days."
x: The hotel charges a non-refundable deposit, so you lose it if you cancel.
Because the flight was non-refundable, they could not get any money back.

opt for.n: Opt for is a phrasal verb meaning to choose one option over others, usually after thinking about the alternatives. It is followed directly by the thing chosen: opt for the cheaper model. A related pattern is opt to followed by a verb: "many people opt to work from home". The verb opt also appears in the phrase opt out, which means to decide not to take part. Opt for is slightly more formal than go for or choose, so it fits essays and reports. When you name the thing chosen, use for rather than of or to: opt for tea, not opt of tea.
x: Many commuters now opt for cycling because it is cheaper and often faster.
If you want a quieter holiday, you could opt for a small island instead.

preserve.n: Preserve means to protect something so it stays in its original condition, and it is used for buildings, traditions, nature and food. Typical objects are heritage, wildlife, language and evidence. As a noun it can also mean jam (strawberry preserves) or an area reserved for wildlife. Compare preserve with conserve, which is often used for saving resources like energy or water. The noun is preservation and the common adjective is preserved. Stress falls on the second syllable: pre-SERVE. Foods can be preserved by drying, salting or freezing.
x: Volunteers work every summer to preserve the wetlands where rare birds nest.
The museum uses special lighting to preserve the paintings for future generations.

readily.n: Readily is an adverb with two main uses. First, it means easily and without difficulty, often before an adjective or past participle: readily available, readily accessible, readily understood. Second, it can mean willingly, as in "she readily admitted her mistake". In both senses it sounds fairly formal. Be careful with word order: readily usually comes before the adjective or between the auxiliary and the main verb. Do not confuse it with ready, an adjective meaning prepared. It is also useful in writing about information, where readily available means you can get it without effort or special permission.
x: Fresh vegetables are readily available at the market, even in the middle of winter.
He readily admitted that he had not read the report before the meeting.

scarce.n: Scarce describes something that exists only in small amounts so that people may not have enough, as with water, food or jobs. The opposite is plentiful. The noun is scarcity, and a phrase you may meet is "make yourself scarce", an informal idiom meaning to leave quickly. Be careful with the adverb scarcely, which means almost not or hardly, as in "scarcely any time". Use scarce for resources and scarcely for degree.
x: Skilled workers are scarce in the region, so employers offer high salaries.
Food became scarce in the city after the roads were closed by heavy snow.

tournament.n: A tournament is a competition in which many players or teams play a series of matches until one wins. It is common in sport and games: a football tournament, a chess tournament, a tennis tournament. You take part in a tournament, enter one, or win one. The usual verbs for organising it are host and hold. The stress falls on the first syllable. Compare it with league, where teams play each other over a whole season, and with championship, which is the title or event for the best.
x: More than sixty teams will compete in the youth tournament this weekend.
She won her first chess tournament at the age of twelve.

accountable.n: Accountable means required to explain your actions and accept responsibility for the result. The usual preposition is to a person or group and for the thing: "accountable to voters for spending". It is commonly used with verbs like hold, remain and be, and in the passive pattern "be held accountable". The noun is accountability. It is stronger than responsible, because it suggests that someone can check your actions and impose a consequence. This makes accountable popular in discussions of governments, companies and managers.
x: Managers should be held accountable for decisions that put workers at risk.
The mayor said she is accountable to local residents, not to private donors.

as requested.n: As requested is a formal phrase used in letters and emails to say you are doing something because the reader asked. It often appears at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma, and the action usually follows: "As requested, I have attached my CV." It may also be extended: as requested in your email, or as previously requested. It is a shortened form of "as you requested", so no subject or object is needed. In informal messages, people would more likely say "as you asked" or "here is what you wanted". It is polite, brief and useful in business writing.
x: As requested, I have attached the updated invoice to this email.
The documents were sent as requested, but we have not yet received confirmation.

conclude.n: Conclude has two uses. It can mean to decide something after thinking about the evidence, usually in the pattern "conclude that": "The report concluded that the policy had failed." It can also mean to end something, such as a meeting or a speech. The first sense is more typical in academic writing, and the noun is conclusion, with in conclusion used to start a final paragraph. Notice that conclude needs a that-clause, not an infinitive, when it means to decide. The stress is on the second syllable, con-CLUDE.
x: After reviewing the data, the researchers concluded that the drug was safe for children.
The festival will conclude on Sunday with a fireworks display over the harbour.

contention.n: Contention is a formal noun with two senses. First, it is a claim or opinion that someone argues for, as in "my main contention is that". Second, it means disagreement, as in a bone of contention, a topic people keep arguing about. In sport and competitions, the phrase in contention means still having a chance to win. The related adjective contentious describes something likely to cause argument. In essays, the sentence "It is my contention that..." is a strong way to introduce a thesis, though it sounds rather formal.
x: It is her contention that public libraries are more important now than ever.
The size of the budget has long been a bone of contention between the two parties.

deposition.n: Deposition has quite different meanings, so context matters. In geography and geology it is the process by which wind, water or ice leave behind sand, soil or rock in a new place, which is the opposite of erosion. In law, a deposition is a formal statement given under oath and recorded outside a courtroom, mainly in American usage. In history it can also mean removing a ruler from power, and the verb for that sense is depose. The verb for the geography meaning is deposit. In a physical geography essay, erosion, transportation and deposition are usually listed as three stages.
x: River deposition creates fertile plains because the water drops its sediment where it slows down.
The witness gave a deposition to the lawyers two weeks before the trial.

extinct.n: Extinct describes a species that no longer has any living members anywhere in the world. It is often used with verbs like become, go and be declared: "the species went extinct". The noun is extinction. It is stronger than endangered or rare, which mean a species still exists but may disappear. Do not use it for a single individual; a species or group is extinct, not one animal. It can also describe a volcano that will not erupt again, as in an extinct volcano. It is not used as a verb.
x: Scientists believe that many frog species could become extinct within a few decades.
The extinct volcano on the island is now a popular walking destination.

from scratch.n: From scratch is an idiom meaning from the very beginning, using nothing that already exists. It usually follows a verb such as start, build, begin or make: "build a company from scratch". In cooking it means you prepare food with basic ingredients rather than a ready-made mix, as in "bake a cake from scratch". The idiom is informal to neutral and is often positive because it suggests effort and independence. Note the fixed preposition from, and do not change scratch into another form. A different idiom, up to scratch, means good enough.
x: After the fire destroyed her shop, she decided to rebuild everything from scratch.
He learned to bake bread from scratch by watching videos online.

literacy.n: Literacy is an uncountable noun meaning the ability to read and write. Because it is uncountable it takes no a or an and no plural: "literacy is improving". It is often used in compounds that mean basic competence in a field, such as digital literacy, financial literacy or media literacy. The related adjective is literate, and the opposite is illiterate, while the noun illiteracy names the lack of the ability. Compare it with numeracy, the ability to work with numbers. Statistics on literacy are often given as a rate or percentage of adults.
x: Programmes to improve adult literacy have helped thousands of people find better jobs.
Digital literacy is now as important as reading and writing for most office jobs.

push back.n: Push back is a phrasal verb with two main meanings. It can mean to move an event to a later time, which is common at work: "We had to push back the meeting." With a noun object you can place it before or after the particle, but a pronoun must go between them: push it back. It can also mean to resist or object, usually in the form push back against something. As a noun, pushback means resistance or criticism. Compared with postpone, the phrasal verb is more informal and is typical of spoken business English.
x: The manager decided to push back the deadline by a week because of the delays.
Local residents have promised to push back against plans for a motorway through the village.

recreation.n: Recreation is an uncountable noun for activities done for enjoyment and relaxation during free time, such as sport, walking or games. It is often found in public contexts, including recreation centre, recreation ground and outdoor recreation. Do not confuse it with re-creation, which is rarely used and means creating something again. The hyphen in re-creation signals this different meaning. The related adjective is recreational, as in recreational facilities or recreational drugs. In casual speech people usually say free time or leisure activities.
x: The council has built a new park to provide space for outdoor recreation.
The town's recreation centre offers swimming lessons, yoga classes and a climbing wall.

symphony.n: A symphony is a long piece of classical music written for a full orchestra, usually in several parts called movements. You compose, conduct, play or perform a symphony, and you often name it by number: Beethoven's Fifth Symphony. The word also appears in symphony orchestra, a large orchestra. Pronounce it SIM-fuh-nee, with the stress on the first syllable and the ph sounded as f. The adjective is symphonic. Do not use symphony for a short song or a band's piece; it needs a large classical form.
x: The orchestra will perform a Mozart symphony in the town hall on Saturday evening.
Writing a symphony took the composer almost three years of hard work.

fortnight.n: Fortnight is a period of fourteen days, or two weeks, and it is much more common in British English than in American English. Americans usually say two weeks. It is used with a: "a fortnight", "in a fortnight", "once a fortnight". The adjective is fortnightly, which can also be an adverb: the magazine appears fortnightly. The word comes from an old phrase meaning fourteen nights. Phrases such as "the past fortnight" and "the next fortnight" are common in British news and conversation.
x: We are going on holiday for a fortnight in August.
The rubbish is collected once a fortnight, so please put the bins out on Monday night.

in advance.n: In advance means before a particular time or event, and it is used when planning, paying or booking: "book in advance", "pay in advance". Another common pattern is "in advance of" followed by a noun, which is more formal, as in "in advance of the election". A related phrase is thank you in advance, used at the end of requests, though some readers find it a little pushy. Do not write in advance with a hyphen. Notice also the adjective advance, as in advance notice or an advance booking, which has no preposition.
x: It is cheaper to buy train tickets in advance rather than on the day.
Please tell us about any dietary requirements in advance so the chef can plan the menu.

convene.n: Convene is a formal verb meaning to call people together for a meeting, or for people to come together for one. It can be transitive or intransitive: "the chair convened a meeting" or "the committee will convene on Monday". Typical objects are a panel, a committee, a hearing, a summit and an inquiry. A person who convenes a meeting is a convener (also convenor). It sounds official, so in ordinary conversation people would say get together or hold a meeting. Stress is on the second syllable, con-VEEN, and the word rhymes with machine.
x: The president will convene a special panel to investigate the cause of the accident.
The committee convenes every month to discuss the city's transport plans.

contradict.n: Contradict means to say or show that something is wrong because it says the opposite, and it can have a person or a statement as its subject: "His account contradicts hers." A person can contradict another person, which can sound rude in conversation. The noun is contradiction and the adjective is contradictory. Reflexive use is also possible: "you are contradicting yourself". Compare it with deny, which means to say something is not true, and with conflict with, which is more neutral. Stress falls on the third syllable: con-tra-DICT.
x: The new figures contradict what the minister said in her speech last week.
Please do not contradict your teacher in front of the whole class.

enable.n: To enable something is to make it possible. The most common pattern is "enable someone to do something": "The app enables users to send money instantly." It can also take a direct object like access or growth. It is stronger and more formal than allow, which can mean give permission, while enable emphasises that something gives the means or ability. The noun is enablement, but it is rare. Do not omit to before the infinitive; "enable people work" is incorrect. Related adjectives such as internet-enabled describe devices that can connect to the web.
x: Online banking enables customers to check their accounts at any time of day.
A scholarship enabled her to study abroad for two years.

evident.n: Evident is a formal adjective meaning clear to see or understand, often used for facts, changes and feelings. It is common in the patterns "it is evident that" and "evident in" or "evident from": "the change is evident in the results". The adverb is evidently, and the noun is evidence, which is uncountable. Be careful with the spelling of evidence, as it ends in -ence. It is close in meaning to obvious, but evident feels more academic and often appears in reports and essays.
x: It was evident from her smile that the interview had gone well.
The influence of the sea is evident in the town's food and architecture.

exclude.n: To exclude someone or something is to leave them out deliberately or to prevent them from taking part. The usual preposition is from: "exclude children from the competition". Data can also be excluded from an analysis. The noun is exclusion, and the adjective is exclusive, which can also mean high-class or limited to a certain group. The opposite is include. The passive is common in official writing: "Tax is excluded from the price".
x: Delivery costs are excluded from the total, so check the final price carefully.
The club does not exclude anyone from joining because of age or experience.

academy.n: Academy has several meanings. It can be a school or college that teaches a particular skill, such as a military academy or a music academy. In England, an academy is also a type of state school run independently of the local council. It can also mean a learned society, for instance the Academy of Sciences. The adjective is academic, with a different stress: a-CAD-e-my for the noun and a-ca-DEM-ic for the adjective. In American English it often appears in names like the Naval Academy.
x: He trained at a football academy for five years before joining a professional club.
The Royal Academy of Arts holds a famous exhibition every summer.

analogy.n: Analogy is a countable noun for a comparison that explains something by showing how it is similar to something else. Typical patterns are "draw an analogy between A and B" and "an analogy with", or "by analogy" for reasoning from a similar case. It differs from a metaphor, because analogy is usually used to explain or argue, while a metaphor is a figure of speech. The adjective is analogous, followed by to or with. A good analogy helps a reader understand a difficult idea quickly.
x: The teacher used an analogy with water pipes to explain how electricity flows.
It is a useful analogy, but it breaks down if you look at the details.

construct.n: A more formal alternative to build, construct means to make or form something. It is used for physical things such as roads, bridges and houses, and also for abstract things like an argument, a theory or a sentence. As a noun, a construct is an idea formed from several parts and the stress shifts to the first syllable: CON-struct. The noun construction means both the process and the thing built. In grammar, a construction is a structure of words. The passive is frequent in news, such as "a new bridge will be constructed".
x: Workers will construct a new bridge across the river over the next two years.
She tried to construct a logical argument from the limited evidence she had.

exceed.n: Numbers, amounts and limits are the usual things you exceed, because the verb means to go beyond them. It takes a direct object with no preposition: exceed the limit, exceed expectations, exceed the budget. The related adjective is excessive, meaning too much, and the noun is excess. It is used in formal contexts such as laws and contracts, for example "drivers must not exceed the speed limit". Note the spelling, with double e in -ceed.
x: Applicants whose essays exceed the word limit will not be considered.
The results exceeded our expectations, so we decided to expand the project.

a ripple effect.n: A ripple effect is a situation in which one event causes a chain of further effects that spread outward, like ripples on water. It usually takes the article a and verbs like have, create or cause: "The strike had a ripple effect across the industry." It is followed by on or across and the affected area. The effect can be positive or negative. It is similar to the knock-on effect, but the image suggests the effects spread gradually outward. In writing, it is used for causes and consequences in economics and society.
x: One small price increase can have a ripple effect throughout the whole supply chain.
The new factory created a ripple effect, bringing jobs to nearby shops and cafes.

be committed to.n: Be committed to means to be fully dedicated to something, and the important point is that to is a preposition here, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing form: "We are committed to improving quality." Writing "committed to improve" is a common mistake. The structure is typical of mission statements and job applications. You can also use be dedicated to or be devoted to in the same way. The noun is commitment, which is often followed by to as well, and it describes a promise or a strong duty.
x: Teachers here are expected to be committed to helping each student reach their potential.
If you want to pass the exam, you have to be committed to practising every day.

combat.n: Combat as a verb means to try to stop something harmful from happening or growing, and it takes a direct object: combat crime, combat poverty, combat climate change. It is more formal than fight and appears often in news and policy writing. As a noun, combat means fighting in war, as in armed combat. As a verb it takes its object directly, so write "combat crime" rather than "combat against crime".
x: New laws were introduced to combat the rising number of online scams.
Doctors are working to combat the spread of the disease in rural villages.

consolidate.n: Consolidate has two main meanings. In business it means to combine several things, such as companies, offices or debts, into a single unit: "consolidate our three offices into one". More generally, it means to make something stronger or more secure, as in consolidate a lead or a position. Students also use it when they review learning to make it firm, for example "consolidate what you have learned". The noun is consolidation. The verb is transitive and often used with into when combining.
x: The bank plans to consolidate its small branches into a few larger offices.
Revision classes help students consolidate what they have learned during the term.

debunk.n: When you debunk a popular belief, story or claim, you show that it is false, exposing it as a myth. Typical objects are myth, theory, rumour and claim: "debunk the myth that". It is usually used for ideas that many people have believed, not for ordinary mistakes. A person who does this is a debunker. Pronounce it dee-BUNK. It is less formal than refute and often appears in journalism, science writing and video titles about common misconceptions.
x: The programme sets out to debunk common myths about healthy eating.
Scientists quickly debunked the rumour that the water was unsafe to drink.

deterrent.n: Anything that makes people less likely to act, because they fear the consequences, can be called a deterrent. It is often followed by to or against: "a deterrent to crime". The usual verb patterns are act as a deterrent and provide a deterrent. The related verb is deter, which is followed by from and an -ing form: "deter people from driving". The adjective is the same word, as in deterrent effect. In politics, a nuclear deterrent means weapons that prevent attack by threatening a response.
x: High fines can be an effective deterrent against dropping litter in the street.
Many experts doubt that harsher punishments act as a deterrent to serious crime.

emission.n: Emission is the production or sending out of gas, heat, light or radiation, and in news it most often means gases from vehicles, factories or power stations. It is very often plural in this sense, as in carbon emissions, greenhouse gas emissions and exhaust emissions. Common verbs are cut, reduce, produce and limit. The verb is emit; note that the noun has one m and a double s. The stress is on the second syllable, e-MISH-un. A target such as net zero emissions means balancing what is emitted with what is removed.
x: The city aims to cut traffic emissions by banning older diesel cars from the centre.
Emissions from the power station fell sharply after it switched to natural gas.

additive.n: An additive is a substance added to something else in small amounts to improve it, preserve it or change its colour or taste. It is most common with food, as in food additive, but it also appears with fuel and plastics. In the EU, food additives are given E numbers. It is not the same as an ingredient, which is a main part of a recipe. The related verb is add and as an adjective it appears in technical phrases such as additive colour mixing. The stress is on the first syllable: AD-i-tiv.
x: Some food additives are used to keep products fresh for much longer.
The label says this juice contains no artificial colours or additives.

boost sales.n: Boost sales means to increase the amount of a product that is sold, and boost is a verb meaning to increase or improve something and give it extra power. In this phrase the object is sales, which is a plural noun used without the. Related patterns are boost profits, boost morale and boost the economy. Typical subjects are discounts, advertising, a campaign or a celebrity. The verb boost is informal-neutral and common in business news. Sales can be boosted by a percentage or to a figure, and "boost up" is unnecessary here.
x: A clever advertising campaign helped the brand boost sales among younger customers.
Free delivery was introduced in order to boost sales during the quiet winter months.

canopy.n: Canopy has a common use in nature writing: the top layer of branches and leaves in a forest, forming a kind of roof. The forest canopy is home to many birds and insects, and the area below is called the understorey. In other contexts, a canopy is a cover over a bed, a doorway or a seat, and it can also be the part of a parachute that opens. The stress is on the first syllable, CAN-o-py. In rainforest descriptions, an emergent tree rises above the canopy.
x: Sunlight barely reaches the forest floor because of the thick canopy of leaves above.
Monkeys and many birds spend almost their whole lives high in the canopy.

commute.n: Commute as a verb means to travel regularly between home and work or school. It can be followed by to and a place, or by an amount of time or a means: "commute to London by train". It is usually used for repeated, daily travel, not a one-off trip. The noun commute is common too, as in a long commute, and the person is a commuter. Note that commute can also mean to reduce a legal punishment, but that sense is mainly legal. Stress is on the second syllable: com-MUTE.
x: She commutes to the city by train, which takes nearly ninety minutes each way.
Fewer people commute to the office every day since remote work became common.

comply with.n: Comply with is a phrasal verb meaning to obey a rule, law, order or standard. The preposition with is required: "comply with the regulations". "Comply the rules" is wrong, and "comply to" is non-standard in careful writing. The noun is compliance, also followed by with, and the adjective is compliant. It sounds formal and is common in workplaces, legal writing and safety notices. Companies often hire compliance officers to check that rules are followed. The opposite phrase is fail to comply.
x: Restaurants must comply with strict hygiene rules or they may be closed.
Anyone who refuses to comply with the safety instructions will be asked to leave.

coniferous.n: Coniferous is an adjective for trees that bear cones, such as pine, spruce and fir, and most of them keep their needle-like leaves all year round. It is usually used with tree or forest: a coniferous forest. The related noun is conifer. Coniferous forests are often contrasted with broad-leaved forests, whose trees are mostly deciduous and lose their leaves in autumn. Strictly, though, deciduous is the opposite of evergreen, and a few conifers, such as the larch, are deciduous too.
x: Coniferous trees such as pines survive cold winters better than many broad-leaved species.
The mountains were covered with dark coniferous forest as far as we could see.

crate.n: A crate is a large strong box used for transporting or storing goods such as fruit, bottles or tools, often made of wood or plastic. It is commonly used with of: a crate of apples. It can also be a container for transporting a pet, a dog crate. As a verb, to crate something means to pack it in a crate. Compare it with box, which is a general word, and case, which is often used for smaller protective containers. A crate of beer usually holds a fixed number of bottles.
x: The workers unloaded forty crates of oranges from the back of the lorry.
We keep our dog in a crate at night so that it feels safe.

dip.n: Dip as a noun means a small fall or decrease, often temporary, in numbers or levels: a dip in sales, a slight dip. It is used with in: "a dip in profits". The same word is also a food noun for a thick sauce used with chips or vegetables, and a short swim, as in "a quick dip in the sea". As a verb it means to go down slightly or to put something briefly into liquid. In graphs, a dip is smaller and shorter than a slump or a collapse.
x: There was a brief dip in unemployment last spring before the rate rose again.
After a short dip in the lake, we sat in the sun to dry.

administrate.n: Administrate means to manage and organise the work or affairs of an organisation, but administer is more common and usually preferred. Administer takes the same objects, such as a programme, a fund or a school. Administrate does exist, but many writers see it as an unnecessary variant. The noun is administration, and a person is an administrator. Note that administer can also mean to give medicine or a test, while administrate does not. If you are unsure, use administer or manage.
x: The charity employs staff to administrate the fund and check how it is spent.
A small team administrates the online library and answers students' questions.

approximately.n: Approximately is an adverb meaning roughly or about, and it is used before numbers, amounts and times: approximately 200 people. It sounds more formal than about or around, so it suits reports and academic writing. Do not combine it with another word of the same meaning, as in "approximately about". The adjective is approximate, and the verb approximate means to come close to a figure. In writing, the abbreviation approx. is used in tables. The stress is on the second syllable, ap-PROX-i-mate-ly.
x: The journey takes approximately three hours, depending on the traffic.
Approximately one third of the students in our survey travel to school by bus.

autopay.n: Autopay is a noun for a service that automatically pays a regular bill from your bank account or card on a set date. It is common in American English; British speakers more often say direct debit. Typical phrases are set up autopay, sign up for autopay and turn off autopay. It is uncountable and usually written as one word, though auto-pay also appears. The benefit is that you will not miss a payment, but you should still check the amount each month. It is an informal consumer term and less typical in formal letters.
x: You can sign up for autopay online and avoid late fees on your electricity bill.
I turned off autopay because the amount changed and I wanted to check it first.

concurrent.n: Concurrent is a formal adjective meaning happening at the same time, and it is often used for processes, sentences, studies or events. The common pattern is concurrent with: "the strike was concurrent with the election". The adverb is concurrently. In law, concurrent sentences are served together rather than one after another. In computing, concurrent processes run during the same period. It is similar to simultaneous, but concurrent often suggests overlapping in time rather than exactly at the same moment.
x: The book fair runs concurrently with the music festival, so the whole town will be busy.
The judge gave him two concurrent sentences of five years each.

i partly agree.n: I partly agree is a polite way to show you accept some of an argument but not all of it, which is very useful in discussions and speaking exams. It is usually followed by with and a person or idea: "I partly agree with you" or "I partly agree with that statement". Then you normally add a contrast with but or however and explain what you disagree with. The adverb partly can also move: "I agree partly" is possible but less natural. Compare it with "I agree to some extent", which has a very similar meaning. Avoid saying only "I partly agree" without giving a reason.
x: I partly agree with your view, but the figures suggest the problem is more complex.
I partly agree that cars should be banned, though many people have no other way to travel.
